full_text:
Andhra Pradesh’s power consumption has fallen sharply after cyclone-induced rainfall lowered temperatures, offering the state temporary relief from the cost and operational pressure of meeting peak electricity demand. The change shows how closely the state’s power system is tied to weather: a few days of extreme heat can push households towards intensive use of air-conditioners and air coolers, while rain can quickly reduce demand.
According to a report by Deccan Chronicle, daily power consumption in Andhra Pradesh stood at 170 million units on Wednesday and 200 million units on Thursday. That was well below the state’s peak demand of 288 million units recorded on May 21. The immediate reduction followed heavy rainfall associated in the report with severe cyclone Arnab, which brought down temperatures after a period of sweltering conditions.
The numbers indicate the scale of the short-term swing. Thursday’s reported consumption was 88 million units below the May peak, a reduction of about 31 per cent. Wednesday’s consumption was 118 million units lower, or roughly 41 per cent below that peak. These figures are daily energy consumption numbers, while the report separately describes the May figure as peak demand. They therefore should not be treated as a direct measure of the same operational indicator, but they still show the pressure created by weather-sensitive electricity use.
The heatwave conditions had increased the use of cooling appliances in homes and other establishments. The report said air-conditioners and air coolers were being used extensively in mid-October as residents attempted to cope with the heat. That increase in consumption came at a time when electricity procurement was expensive and availability in the open market was not assured for every state.
For a power utility, the issue is not only how much electricity is consumed over a day. It is also when demand rises, how much generation is available at that time, and what the utility must pay to secure additional supply. The report said Andhra Pradesh had purchased power at prices ranging from Rs 15 to Rs 20 per unit during peak hours. It also stated that power was ideally purchased at between Rs 6 and Rs 10 per unit during peak hours and at up to Rs 2.50 per unit during non-peak hours.
This difference makes weather a financial variable for the electricity system. When temperatures rise, cooling demand can increase during already stressed periods. If the state’s contracted or internal generation is insufficient, the utility may have to buy additional power at a higher market price. When rainfall lowers temperatures, that immediate procurement pressure can ease. The reduction in consumption therefore provides financial relief, but it does not eliminate the underlying exposure to extreme-weather demand spikes.
The report said Andhra Pradesh has base power-generation availability ranging from 8,900 megawatts to 9,100 megawatts to support round-the-clock supply. It added that solar power can be used during the afternoon when additional electricity is needed, while hydel-electric power can be used at night. The distinction points to the importance of timing in managing the grid: different sources become useful at different parts of the day, and the value of a source depends not only on its installed capacity but also on when it can deliver electricity.
Andhra Pradesh’s installed total power capacity was reported at nearly 21,800 megawatts. This includes about 6,600 megawatts from thermal power, 1,780 megawatts from hydel power, 8,500 megawatts from solar and wind, 2,000 megawatts from central generating stations and 1,600 megawatts from independent power producers, with the balance coming from other sources.
These figures also show why installed capacity and available supply cannot be read as identical. The total installed capacity across all sources is substantially higher than the base availability cited for routine supply. The supplied report does not explain the difference between the two measures or specify the availability of each generation source at particular times. It does, however, make clear that the state relies on a combination of its own generation, central stations, independent producers, renewable sources and power purchases.
The composition of the installed capacity is significant for managing weather-linked demand. Thermal power provides a major part of the reported capacity, while solar and wind together account for a larger figure in the report’s breakdown. Hydel power is a smaller component but is identified as a source that can be used at night when additional supply is required. The report does not provide plant-level availability, transmission constraints, reserve margins or the actual contribution of each source during the recent heatwave. Those gaps limit what can be concluded about the system’s technical resilience.
The state’s procurement arrangements are another important part of the picture. State energy authorities told the publication that Andhra Pradesh had signed agreements with power plants to secure supply until August 2027. The report also quoted Andhra Pradesh power grid director AKV Bhaskar as saying that daily consumption had fallen in parts of the state after the heavy rainfall and that power could be obtained from power plants until the following August even if demand rose again.
The report contains a discrepancy in the description of this timeline: it refers to agreements extending up to August 2027, while the quoted official statement refers to availability until the following August. The precise contractual period and the volume of power covered are not established in the supplied material. What is clear from the report is that the state is relying on advance arrangements to reduce its exposure to uncertain short-term purchases.
This is particularly relevant because electricity demand is becoming more sensitive to heat in areas where households and businesses use mechanical cooling. The report links the recent increase in demand to air-conditioners and air coolers, but it does not provide appliance ownership data, feeder-level demand figures or a longer time series. It is therefore not possible from the supplied evidence to determine whether the reported May peak was part of a sustained trend or an exceptional event.
The weather outlook described in the report added another short-term factor. The India Meteorological Department was said to have forecast another spell of rainfall in coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema and Yanam over the next four days up to November 3, following the formation of a low-pressure area over the south Andaman Sea and adjoining areas. If the reported rainfall occurred, it could keep temperatures and electricity demand lower in the immediate period. The supplied material does not establish how much demand would change or whether the rain would affect generation and distribution operations.
The geography mentioned in the forecast also matters for interpreting the state-wide numbers. Andhra Pradesh contains coastal and inland regions with different weather conditions, while Yanam is a separate Union Territory enclave administered as part of Puducherry. The report says consumption had fallen in parts of Andhra Pradesh, but it does not provide a district-level comparison. A state-wide figure can therefore conceal variation between areas that receive rain and those that remain hot.
The immediate lesson is that power planning must account for both supply capacity and demand volatility. A utility can have a large installed capacity and still face financial and operational stress when high temperatures push demand up faster than available supply. Conversely, a fall in demand after rainfall can reduce the need for expensive purchases without changing the underlying capacity of the system.
The report presents Andhra Pradesh as being in a relatively secure position because of its supply agreements, even as some other states faced limited availability in the open market. That assessment is attributed to the report and state energy authorities; the supplied material does not provide a comparative table or independent assessment of other states’ procurement positions. The evidence supports a narrower conclusion: Andhra Pradesh had arrangements that authorities believed would help it manage a renewed rise in demand.
The larger urban question is how electricity systems should prepare for weather that can quickly alter household demand. In this case, rainfall functioned as a temporary demand-reduction mechanism, while the preceding heat acted as a stress test for procurement and availability. Neither condition resolves the longer-term question of how much dependable power is available during extreme heat, how much it costs, and whether supply can reach the areas where cooling demand rises most sharply.
The available evidence confirms three immediate facts: Andhra Pradesh’s reported electricity consumption declined after temperatures fell, the state had recorded a much higher demand figure earlier, and authorities cited a mix of generation capacity and supply agreements as protection against another increase. The report does not establish the duration of the decline, the exact contractual volumes, the impact on consumer tariffs or the performance of individual generation sources. Those are the indicators that would be needed to determine whether the recent relief represents a short weather-driven fluctuation or a broader improvement in the state’s power-supply position.
